title: Why a Mars analog gives each crewmate a door
summary: A tour of NASA’s CHAPEA layout shows which activities share a room and which need their own space.
heading: A home and a workplace
body: Four volunteers share Mars Dune Alpha in Houston. Each has private quarters, while the crew shares a kitchen and dedicated areas for exercise, medical care, growing crops and work. Someone preparing dinner and someone finishing a work shift can occupy different parts of the same small building.
application: For a future outpost, try tracing two routes through the habitat: a tired crewmate heading to bed and a colleague going to exercise. Where the paths meet matters as much as floor area. CHAPEA lets researchers study daily life in that layout under isolation on Earth.
claim: The four-person CHAPEA habitat includes individual crew quarters and shared work and recreation areas.

title: A room that travels folded
summary: The BEAM experiment tested whether a spacecraft could gain usable interior space after launch.
heading: From cargo to room
body: A launch vehicle has limited room under its fairing. The Bigelow Expandable Activity Module travelled to the International Space Station in a compact configuration. After attachment, it expanded into a pressurized room that astronauts could enter.
discussion: What the trial tells a habitat designer
application: Launching a room compactly and monitoring it after expansion addresses a real transport constraint. A designer applying that idea on Mars would also have to account for landing, contact with the ground and dust. BEAM supplies evidence about an expandable module in orbit.
claim: BEAM expanded after attachment to the International Space Station.

title: How MOXIE made oxygen from Martian air
summary: A rover experiment demonstrated that Mars’s atmosphere can supply raw material for oxygen production.
heading: An experiment at Jezero Crater
body: MOXIE aboard Perseverance drew in Martian air and separated oxygen from carbon dioxide. Across sixteen runs it produced 122 grams of oxygen. That total describes the entire experiment, so it should not be read as an hourly production rate.
discussion: From a sample to a supply
application: NASA identifies a further challenge for a future mission: collecting and storing the product. A crew planning a reserve would need to know how much oxygen is in storage, how fast the system replenishes it and how much power is available between runs.
sourceTitle: NASA’s Oxygen-Generating Experiment MOXIE Completes Mars Mission
claim: MOXIE produced a cumulative 122 grams of oxygen during sixteen runs on Mars.

title: How station water becomes breathing oxygen
summary: On the ISS, the water processor and oxygen generator perform different jobs in the same life-support system.
heading: Two steps in the loop
body: The station recovers water from several streams, including cabin humidity and processed urine. After treatment, part of the clean supply can feed the oxygen generator. Electricity splits water into oxygen and hydrogen, and the oxygen enters the cabin atmosphere.
application: Imagine a habitat with water in a collection tank while its treatment unit is offline. The tank level alone says little about how much water can reach the oxygen generator. Following water through each stage helps explain why two inventories, recovered water and usable water, can tell different stories.
sourceTitle: Environmental Control and Life Support Systems (ECLSS)
claim: The station’s oxygen generation assembly splits water by electrolysis.

title: Packing a meal for the last month on Mars
summary: A menu for a long expedition has to stay nutritious and appealing long after launch.
heading: What happens between deliveries
body: ISS crews occasionally receive fresh food on cargo flights. A Mars expedition would go much longer between opportunities to resupply. Food planners therefore consider storage life alongside nutrition, the space each package occupies and whether crews will want to eat it.
application: Consider a menu with a favourite item that keeps for only part of the mission. Moving it to the first months solves its storage problem but leaves fewer choices later. Reviewing the menu month by month makes that trade visible before food is packed.
sourceTitle: Risk of Inadequate Food and Nutrition
claim: Longer exploration missions require food that remains suitable through longer intervals without resupply.

title: Growing a salad inside a spacecraft
summary: The ISS Veggie garden shows what a small fresh crop needs inside a controlled cabin.
heading: Inside a plant pillow
body: In Veggie, roots grow in small pillows containing a growing medium and fertilizer. Water and air must reach the roots, while LEDs illuminate the leaves. Crews have grown leafy vegetables including lettuce and mizuna in this compact system.
discussion: What to put on the menu
application: A harvest can add a fresh ingredient to a stored meal. Planning an entire menu around that harvest raises a different question: what will everyone eat while the next leaves grow? The ISS experiment demonstrates one way to supplement provisions and gives planners concrete tasks to budget, including watering and tending plants.
claim: Veggie has grown leafy vegetables in plant pillows under LED lighting aboard the ISS.

title: What dust cost InSight’s solar panels
summary: Two measurements from the same lander show how much a daily power budget can change.
heading: Two readings from Mars
body: Soon after landing, InSight’s solar panels supplied about 5,000 watt-hours per sol. By spring 2022, accumulated dust had reduced that figure to about 500. A watt-hour measures energy, so these numbers can be compared with the energy needed to operate an instrument over a day.
application: The later figure is about one tenth of the earlier one. In an outpost planning exercise, try assigning the same daily tasks to both budgets. The shortfall illustrates the danger of treating landing-day production as a guaranteed supply throughout a mission.
sourceTitle: InSight’s Power Generation: After Landing and Spring 2022
claim: InSight’s daily solar energy fell from about 5,000 to about 500 watt-hours per sol between landing and spring 2022.

title: Where Perseverance gets power after sunset
summary: Perseverance carries a generator whose heat serves two purposes on Mars.
heading: Heat, current and storage
body: The rover’s radioisotope generator converts part of the heat released by natural radioactive decay into electrical energy. It charges two batteries. Heat from the system also helps keep rover hardware within its operating temperature range.
discussion: Three entries in an energy budget
application: A useful way to read a rover diagram is to trace electricity produced now, energy stored for later and heat carried to cold equipment. Each has a different use. The rover demonstrates that distinction on Mars, while a crewed habitat would need its own estimates of demand.
claim: Perseverance uses a radioisotope generator to charge batteries and help keep equipment warm.

title: Why a space toilet separates waste streams
summary: The ISS toilet routes liquid and solid waste differently from the moment of collection.
heading: Collection in microgravity
body: Airflow helps carry waste away from the user. The space toilet collects urine through a funnel and hose, while solid waste enters a separate container. On the station, the liquid stream can go on to water recovery.
application: For a surface habitat, draw the route from each collection point to its destination. A liquid processing unit and a solid storage container have different capacity limits. Mars has gravity, so the ISS arrangement is a reference for separating streams rather than a complete surface toilet design.
sourceTitle: NASA’s New Space Toilet Offers More Comfort, Improved Efficiency for Deep Space Missions
claim: ISS toilet systems collect urine separately from solid waste and direct urine toward water recovery.

title: Turning loose trash into tiles
summary: NASA has tested a way to reduce the volume occupied by everyday spacecraft rubbish.
heading: What a compactor changes
body: Food wrappers and other discarded items occupy cabin storage even after their contents have been used. NASA’s Heat Melt Compactor applies heat and pressure to suitable trash to form dense tiles. A regular shape makes the processed material easier to stow.
discussion: Volume and mass answer different questions
application: Imagine marking the storage space occupied by a bag of wrappers before and after compaction. A smaller outline means more room is available. The material in the tile still needs a destination, so an outpost plan should track both the space recovered and the tiles accumulated.
sourceTitle: What is NASA’s Heat Melt Compactor?
claim: NASA’s Heat Melt Compactor uses heat and pressure to turn suitable trash into compact tiles.

title: Working together when Earth cannot answer immediately
summary: The CHAPEA crew rehearsed both delayed messages and a planned loss of contact.
heading: A question in transit
body: In a CHAPEA analog mission, one-way messages were normally delayed by three to twenty-three minutes. The team also experienced a simulated two-week communications outage. During that interval they continued activities inside the habitat without routine guidance from mission control.
application: Consider a crop problem that the next shift will inherit before Earth replies. A handover can record what the crew observed, what has already been tried and what decision is still open. The next shift can then continue from the same evidence, and Earth can respond to a specific question when contact returns.
claim: CHAPEA simulated a two-week loss of communication in addition to routine message delays.

title: What a day off looks like in an isolated habitat
summary: Crew accounts from Mars Dune Alpha describe how people spent time together after work.
heading: After the shift
body: In NASA’s account of the first CHAPEA mission, the crew normally worked five and a half days each week. They also described ways of unwinding inside the habitat. A long stay therefore includes recurring decisions about shared space and free time as well as assignments from mission control.
application: Picture an evening when one person wants quiet and others want a shared activity. A schedule that identifies common rooms and private time gives the group a practical way to accommodate both. The CHAPEA account offers an example of life in isolation on Earth that a future surface crew could discuss.
sourceTitle: A Year in Mars Dune Alpha
claim: The first CHAPEA crew described a typical five-and-a-half-day working week in the analog habitat.
